Items.Authors: Peter D. Miller, Joshua Abel, Matthew Bolcar, Bente Eegholm, Jesse Huguet, Josh Johnson, Alden Jurling, Nicole Lewis, Alice Liu, Brian Martens, Jacob Massey, Pete McCarthy, Scott Paine, J. Scott Smith
Items.Title: Optical stability of the Roman Optical Telescope assembly
Items.Abstract: The Roman Space Telescope is a three-mirror anastigmat design with a 2.4 m primary mirror, which will provide science information on dark energy and exoplanets via two science instruments. The Optical Telescope Assembly (OTA) collects and conditions light for both the Widefield Instrument (WFI) and Coronagraph Instrument (CGI). Optical stability is a critical performance aspect of the OTA that enables the science objectives of both instruments. The program prioritized optical stability from the beginning through to final delivery, encompassing requirements, design, analysis, model validation, testing, and verification. After completing final optical testing and shipping the OTA to Goddard Space Flight Center in October 2024, final predictions for on-orbit optical stability were made. The OTA is expected to far exceed its optical stability requirements, with analysis predicting sub-nanometer stability over several days.

Items.Authors: Jake D. Hutchinson, Robert Spry, Adam D. Wilkinson, Cédric Pereira, John-Paul Walker, David de Castro Alves, Robert Watkins, Rebecca Holleb, Emma Ryan, Waqas Mir, Greg King, Keith Nowicki, Roy Preece, Fraser Clarke, Manuel Abreu, Neil Bowles
Items.Title: Optomechanical design of a broadband cryogenic optical system for ground testing of the Ariel payload
Items.Abstract: In this proceeding, the optical and opto-mechanical design of the optical ground support equipment (OGSE) for TVAC testing of the Ariel payload is described. Analysis is presented to demonstrate that the OGSE is capable of meeting stringent optical quality requirements upon cooling to an operating temperature of 70 K. This facilitates a host of performance tests of the Ariel telescope and instruments prior to integration with the spacecraft.

Items.Authors: Marc-Antoine Martinod, Michael J. Ireland, Denis Defrère, Stefan Kraus, Frantz Martinache, Peter G. Tuthill, Emilie Bouzerand, Julia Bryant, Sorabh Chhabra, Peter Chingaipe, Benjamin Courtney-Barrer, Fred Crous, Nick Cvetojevic, Daniel Dahl, Colin Dandumont, Steve Ertel, Germain Garreau, Adrian M. Glauser, Xavier Haubois, Lucas Labadie, Stéphane Lagarde, Daniel Lancaster, Romain Laugier, Roxanne Ligi, Nathan Long, Alexandra Mazzoli, Thomas Mattheussen, Gyorgy Medgyesi, Kwinten Missiaen, Sebastien Morel, Daniel Ahrer, Barnaby Norris, Jyortimay Paul, Romain Petrov, Gert Raskin, Sylvie Robbe-Dubois, Gordon Robertson, Muhammad Salman, Ahmed Sanny, Nicolas Schuhler, Owain Snaith, Adam Taras
Items.Title: Pushing high angular resolution and high contrast observations on the VLTI from Y to L band with the Asgard instrumental suite: progress status and plans
Items.Abstract: ESO’s VLTI has a history of record-breaking discoveries in astrophysics using high-angular resolution instrumentation. Its latest visitor instrument, the Asgard instrumental suite, is one key to further enhance the potential of the facility, particularly in the very near-infrared. It comprises four natively collaborating instruments: HEIMDALLR, a K-band fringe tracker, wavefront corrector and stellar interferometer in K band, with the same optics; Baldr, an H-band Zernike wavefront sensor; BIFROST, an Y-J-H-band photonic combiner whose main science case is studying the formation processes and properties of stellar and planetary systems; and NOTT, an L-band nulling interferometer for imaging young planetary systems. The integration of Asgard is planned in three phases. The first one (integration, commissioning of HEIMDALLR and Baldr) is successfully done. We detail the current integration status of the project, the control software, and the next milestone on the roadmap of Asgard.

Items.Authors: Ramon Valles, David Soldevila, Diego Torres, Enrique Mestre, Daniela Hadasch, Igor Oya, Matthias Füßling, Christian Blum
Items.Title: The scheduler systems of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
Items.Abstract: This presentation outlines the scheduling systems that enable the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) to manage its large, distributed array of telescopes and diverse scientific proposals. It introduces the multi-layered scheduling pipeline: the Long-, Mid-, and Short-Term schedulers, which automates the observatory operations (planning, scheduling, maintenance, and execution). The talk also highlights the integration of the STARS Core library, which provides advanced optimization and AI techniques to enhance telescope allocation and improve scientific return.

Items.Authors: Emily Hunting, William McBride, Jayadev Rajagopal
Items.Title: Continued vibration analysis and mitigation at the WIYN Telescope
Items.Abstract: Following previous vibration analysis, this work explores the effects of mitigating major sources of vibration in the mount and instrument ports of the WIYN 3.5m Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona, USA. The modeling techniques and mitigation strategies in this work are applicable across NOIRLab and to other observatories seeking to improve image stabilization and are of particular importance for closed-loop tip-tilt correction systems. At WIYN, this translates to increased guiding and fiber coupling efficiency with the NEID extreme precision radial velocity spectrograph. We detail the major maintenance and upgrades undertaken to reduce harmful telescope vibrations. Then we assess the impact on vibrations originating from equipment and the wind and discuss potential next steps. This work is a continuation of a project previously presented at this conference (McBride et al. 2023).

Items.Authors: Kevin Kouwenhoven, Pieter van Zweeden, Shahab Dabironezare, Daan Roos, Wilbert Ras-Vinke, Anthony H. M. Coppens, Daniela Perez Capelo, Dimitry Lamers, Hendrik Veen, David Thoen, Jochem Baselmans, Pieter de Visser
Items.Title: KIDs for LIFE: Efficient mid-infrared single photon counting detectors from 4 to 20 μm
Items.Abstract: The Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE) mission will utilize a mid-infrared nulling interferometer to obtain exoplanet emission spectra from 4-20 μm, producing low photon fluxes per pixel at the spectrograph output. This demands detectors with low noise, high stability, and high optical efficiency across the full LIFE band. Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs), superconducting resonators capable of single-photon detection from the visible to the MIR, offer intrinsic energy resolution, negligible read noise, and dark count rates below 0.1 Hz. Using an aluminum meandering wire-grid absorber on a membrane, we optimize each pixel for its target spectral wavelength. We present MIR KID efficiency measurements at 10 and 18.5 μm using a cryogenic blackbody, and steps towards high quantum efficiency designs compatible with linear arrays for future MIR spectrographic instruments.

Items.Authors: Hein Zelle, John Swinbank
Items.Title: Synergy in data processing pipelines between two observatories
Items.Abstract: In this paper we aim to foster collaboration and create synergy in  data processing and pipeline development between the LOFAR and SKA  observatories. This is done by by defining a common technological  framework for building and executing pipelines. We present our  approach to align data processing software and data infrastructure  across observatories, discussing both technologies under consideration  and how we organise ourselves to maximise the opportunities for  joint development of pipeline software across different teams.

Items.Authors: Norbert Meidinger, Alexander Altmann, Valeria Antonelli, Thomas F. Bechteler, Vadim Burwitz, David Fink, Carlo Fiorini, Max Goretti, Isabell Keil, Pia Knopp, Peter H. Lechner, Jonas W. Muegge, Kirpal Nandra, Rafael Strecker
Items.Title: The detectors for the SFA instrument of the enhanced x-ray timing and polarimetry (eXTP) satellite mission
Items.Abstract: The enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry (eXTP) space science mission is designed to study fundamental physics under extreme conditions of matter density, gravity, and magnetism.   The mission has already been approved in China, with the satellite launch scheduled for 2030.    According to the adopted mission profile, there are two main instruments on eXTP, the Spectroscopy Focusing Array (SFA) and the Polarimetry Focusing Array (PFA).  The spectroscopy focusing array (SFA) instrument will be equipped with 6 telescopes. While each telescope will be equipped with optics of Wolter I type, the focal plane will comprise two different types of spectroscopic detectors: 5 silicon drift detectors (SDDs), each with 19 cells, to enable observations with high time resolution (SFA-T), and 1 spectroscopic PN-CCD detector to allow for imaging and to improve the sensitivity for faint sources (SFA-I).  We present the two types of spectroscopic detectors and their current state of development.

Items.Authors: Haitao Li, Xinyi He, Jinlian Ma, Hui Zhang, Jian Ge, Yan Li
Items.Title: The effects of intra-pixel response on the photometry of the ET mission
Items.Abstract: The Earth 2.0 (ET) mission seeks Earth-like exoplanets in habitable zones of Sun-like stars via transits, requiring tens-of-ppm photometric precision. Systematic noise from intra-/inter-pixel response non-uniformity and pointing jitter dominates the error budget. We performed end-to-end simulations using a super-Gaussian pixel response model parameterized by shape index n (edge sharpness) and central plateau FWHM, combined with realistic jitter, thermal drift, dynamic aberrations, momentum unloading, and diffuse PSFs. Results show higher n yields more rectangular pixel response, and larger plateau width expands the flat region; both strongly suppress motion-induced noise, significantly improving 6.5-hour CDPP. Optimized pixel response uniformity substantially mitigates systematics, confirming that precise control of detector flat-field response is critical for ET to achieve the precision needed to detect transiting Earth analogs around solar-type stars.

Items.Authors: Carel H. D. R. van Gend, Stephen B. Potter, Nicolas Erasmus, Paul Rabe, Hannah Worters, Daniel Cunnama, Roufurd Julie, Robert Firth, Adriano Agnello, Chris Chen, Ciaron Howell, James Todd, Arsalan Yasir, Hazel Martindale, Ruby George, Stefan Marin, Emma Young, Shweta Varadarajan, Chellappa Kannabiran, Darshita Budhadev, Pedro Cavestany-Olivares
Items.Title: Building the Intelligent Observatory
Items.Abstract: We describe the progress made in building the Intelligent Observatory (IO), a program to modernise and improve the efficiency of the facilities and operations of the South African Astronomical Observatory (SAAO). We discuss hardware and software improvements made, our queue-scheduled observation system and how this positions the community to participate in follow-ups to the expected flood of newly discovered transients. Lastly, we describe our application of AI technologies towards improving maintenance and operations, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system to assist users in finding the appropriate system information from a very large body of documentation.

Items.Authors: Sam Ragland, Guido Brusa, Alessandro Cavallaro, Juan Carlos Guerra, Michael Lefebvre, Doug Miller, Jennifer Power, Greg Taylor, Xianyu Zhang, Alexander Becker, Roberto Biasi, Jared Carlson, Patrick Hartley, Joannah Hinz, Elena Masciadri, Brandon Mechtley, Dan Rapoza, Justin Rupert, Joseph Shields, Manu Singh, Christian Veillet
Items.Title: Optimizing and Modernizing Adaptive Optics Operations at the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Large Binocular Telescope Observatory (LBTO) employs advanced Adaptive Optics (AO) technologies, including adaptive secondary mirrors and pyramid wavefront sensors. This paper highlights recent impressive AO science from LBTO and discusses AO operational strategies, along with ongoing efforts to enhance the robustness and efficiency of the AO systems. It summarizes system performance monitoring and calibration strategies. The effects of atmospheric seeing variability on system robustness, efficiency, and performance are examined. Statistics on success rates and elapsed times for each step of target acquisition and AO performance optimization, as well as detailed fault analysis, are provided. Ongoing efforts to improve turbulence monitoring and its influence on planning and executing AO observations are also discussed. Our main goal is to simplify AO operations and minimize the resources and expertise required to operate LBTO’s complex AO systems.

Items.Authors: Thomas Delker, Benjamin Cromey, Derek Sabatke, Jeanette Domber, Maxime Rizzo
Items.Title: Roman Space Telescope wide-field instrument opto-mechanical delivery summary
Items.Abstract: The Wide Field Instrument (WFI) on NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was delivered to Goddard Space Flight Center in the summer of 2024 from its testing at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado. This paper describes the development and qualification process of the Cold Module, which consists of a hexapod adjustment mechanism for the focal plane, an optical element select mechanism, the optical metering support structure within WFI, and the two-stage cooling system. We review the co-development process with Goddard Space Flight Center and discuss each development phase, spanning requirements, design, the physical build, subsystem testing, and integrated instrument testing. Finally, we provide a summary of the technical challenges encountered and their implemented solutions.

Items.Authors: Martin J. Booth
Items.Title: Adaptive optics for high-resolution microscopy: going faster, smaller and deeper
Items.Abstract: I will review recent work on using adaptive optics to increase the capabilities of high-resolution optical microscopy. In particular, I will show how adaptive aberration correction and dynamic phase modulation can improve precision and reliability and increase the accessible volume and speed of these systems. Dependent on the specific application, deformable mirrors, liquid crystal spatial light modulators and other correction devices have been employed. I will outline how new approaches to wavefront measurement have been developed for microscopical applications. These imaging methods have been deployed in wide ranging applications in cell biology, neuroscience and super-resolution microscopy, amongst others.

Items.Authors: Michael P. Fitzgerald, Ashley Baker, Robert Bertz, David B. Brearly, Benjamin Calvin, Therese Cook, Greg Doppmann, Jocelyn Ferrara, Jason Fucik, Rose Gibson, Timothee Greffe, Michael Gutierrez, Samuel Halverson, Takeru Hayashi, Christopher Johnson, Nemanja Jovanovic, Marc Kassis, Quinn Konopacky, Takayuki Kotani, Evan Kress, Michael Langmayr, Kenneth Magnone, Dimitri Mawet, Ricardo Meneses, Reston B. Nash, Bradley Price, Roger Smith, Eric Wang, James H. Wiley, Truman Wold, Jake H. Zimmer
Items.Title: The design and fabrication status of the HISPEC spectrometer system
Items.Abstract: HISPEC is a new high-resolution (R>100,000) near-infrared (NIR) diffraction-limited spectrometer enabling forefront exoplanet characterization in the near infrared (0.98 – 2.46 μm). Its backend consists of a pair of fiber-fed backend echelle spectrometers within independent cryostats spanning the yJ and HK infrared bands. Within each, light from single-mode fibers is collimated, dispersed, and re-imaged onto a Hawaii-4RG. Diffraction-limited optics consist of a collimator/camera pair of gold-coated Zerodur TMAs and gold-coated single-crystal Ge diffraction gratings. There are no moving parts and we primarily use the extremely stable Invar-36 alloy. Each cryostat is cooled by a low-vibration pulse-tube cryocooler. Extensive thermal ballast and a multi-point active control system provide thermo-mechanical stability. Here we present the spectrometer design, review prototyping results, and comment on the status of fabrication, integration, and testing.

Items.Authors: Lorenzo Amati, Enrico Bozzo, Diego Götz, Paul T. O'Brien, Andrea Santangelo
Items.Title: The Transient High-Energy Sky and Early Universe Surveyor (THESEUS) space mission concept and study as ESA/M7 candidate
Items.Abstract: The Transient High-Energy Sky and Early Universe Surveyor (THESEUS) is a mission concept  under study by ESA since 2018 and currently one of  the three candidate M7 mission for a launch in the late '30s. THESEUS aims at fully exploiting  Gamma-Ray Bursts for investigating the Cosmic Dawn and as key phenomena for multi-messenger  astrophysics. By providing an unprecedented combination of X-/gamma-ray monitors, on-board IR  telescope and spacecraft autonomous fast slewing capabilities, THESEUS will be a wonderful  machine for the detection, multi-wavelength characterization and redshift measurement of any kind  of GRBs and many classes of X-ray transients, including high-redshift GRBs for cosmology  and electromagnetic counterparts to sources of gravitational waves. In all thses respects, THESEUS will thus provide an ideal synergy with the very large astronomical facilitiesof the future working in the e.m. (e.g., ELT, CTA, SKA, Athena) and multi-messenger domains (GW, neutrinos).

Items.Authors: Marco Iacobelli, Roberto Pizzo, Hanno Holties, Aida Ahmadi, Aras Bozkurt, Vlad Kondratiev, Emanuela Orrú, Noa Peters, Aleksandar Shulevski, Emma van der Wateren
Items.Title: Early operations with the LOFAR data processing system
Items.Abstract: The LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) telescope is undergoing a major upgrade which will set it in the next decade among the most data intensive astronomical facilities. Therefore the existing data infrastructure is evolving to become cost-effective and to enable scientific productivity. Sustainable science operations will rely on a robust data processing framework distributed on several data centers forming the backbone of the LOFAR science archive, automated quality assurance processes, as well as on efficient computing pipelines. To build and gain experience with operating such a complex system a pathfinder has been set, the ongoing LOFAR Data Valorisation (LDV) project. With this contribution the current status of developments of a scalable, distributed data processing framework will be discussed, as well as the testing of the implemented workflows to generate Advanced Data Products (ADPs). Finally, an overview of the achieved operational results of the last two years will be given.

Items.Authors: Frantz Martinache, Michael J. Ireland, Adam K. Taras, Benjamin Courtney-Barrer, Sylvie Robbe-Dubois, Roxanne Ligi, Nick Cvetojevic, Romain Petrov, Peter G. Tuthill
Items.Title: Heimdallr: integration and commissioning of the VLTI/Asgard fringe-tracker and K-band interferometric instrument
Items.Abstract: Like high-contrast imaging, long-baseline interferometry demands precise upstream metrology. To support two upcoming VLTI/Asgard instruments—the J-band Bifrost spectro-interferometer and the L-band Nott nuller—we implemented Heimdallr, a dual-band (K1–K2) 2D image-plane interferometric recombiner. Heimdallr simultaneously monitors group and phase delays, tip-tilt, and pupil excursions that would otherwise cause coupling losses into downstream single-mode photonic combiners. Integrated with the Baldr focal AO stage and the Solarstein calibration source, Heimdallr was assembled at Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur (Oct 2024–Apr 2025), reassembled at Paranal (July 2025), and commissioned on the VLTI AT array (Sept 2025). We present Heimdallr’s operational modes—fringe tracking, tip‑tilt tracking, and pupil‑drift alignment—its ability to provide standalone visibilities and closure phases, and commissioning performance based on integration and on‑sky data, including results down to mK = 9.5.

Items.Authors: Gary Donegan, Cáthal McAleer, Colm Bracken, Oisín Creaner, Mario De Lucia, Tom Ray, Gerhard Ulbricht
Items.Title: Optimization of TiN / Ti / TiN triple-layer optical to near-IR Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors
Items.Abstract: We are developing MKIDs for the optical to near IR range made from TiN / Ti / TiN triple layers, utilizing the superconducting proximity effect to fine-tune the superconducting energy gap, achieving good control of critical temperature and good homogeneity. We will present our efforts to optimize the fabrication process of photon counting MKIDs. We will report on measured internal and coupling quality factors, and their dependency on temperature, drive power and Ti to TiN ratio. We will also report on improved signal strength and photon wavelength resolution facilitated varying inductor volumes such that the total number of Cooper Pairs is changed to achieve varying signals strengths from incident photons breaking the same number of pairs.

Items.Authors: Lionel Clermont, Celine Michel, Christian Kintziger, Wilfried Uhring, Pascal Blain
Items.Title: Revealing stray light in time: the time-of-flight approach for space instruments characterization
Items.Abstract: Stray light has emerged as one of the most critical challenges for high-performance space telescopes. Conventional on-ground characterization methods are slow, costly, and inherently blind to the full complexity of stray-light behavior. They rely on brute-force testing, often missing features and failing to reveal stray light physical origins. As a result, performance requirements are not always met on-ground, and unexpected stray-light issues may still appear once in orbit. The Time-of-Flight (ToF) stray-light characterization technique breaks this impasse by introducing time as a new metrology dimension. It enables the detection of even the faintest contributions together with their physical origin, allowing precise identification and efficient resolution of potential problems. This presentation will showcase the latest developments of the technique, discuss implementation strategies and outline the next steps of the technology roadmap supported by an ERC-funded research program.

Items.Authors: Corey D. Packard, Logan Canull, Jacob Wainio, Mark D. Klein, Javier Romualdez, Peter Bartosik
Items.Title: Thermal validation of a balloon-borne infrared telescope (EXCITE) using test flight measurement data and TAITherm
Items.Abstract: The EXoplanet Climate Infrared TElescope will study the atmospheres of exoplanets, collecting infrared data for phase-resolved spectroscopy during circumpolar scientific balloon missions. Helium balloon-borne altitudes up to 40 kilometers allow for observations with minimal deleterious atmospheric effects, but these infrared measurements require a proper thermal envelope for sensitive astronomical instrumentation. A thermal model of the balloon-tethered gondola and payload was constructed, a steady state polar orbit condition and a transient ascent scenario were simulated, and a design study explored material and surface property choices. Subsequently, a successful test flight was performed in August 2024 from New Mexico. During this test flight, temperature data was collected on the gondola and telescope. In this work we compare transient temperature predictions to in-flight measurement data. We present the results and conclusions of this high-altitude thermal validation.

Items.Authors: Imad Pasha, Roberto G. Abraham, William P. Bowman, Seery Chen, Steven Janssens, Deborah Lokhorst, Carter Rhea, Lisa Sloan, Pieter van Dokkum
Items.Title: Autonomous software infrastructure for the 1140 unit massively distributed MOTHRA observatory
Items.Abstract: We describe the autonomous observing software powering MOTHRA, a distributed aperture array of 1140 high-end telephoto lenses equipped with tiltable ultra-narrow interference filters, CMOS cameras, and raspberry pi computers. When completed, the system will be optically-equivalent to a 4.7m f/0.08 refractor with an eight square degree field of view, operating as an R=800 integral field unit. Here we present the software and network architecture that drives the array's autonomous operations, including the scheduling of observing activities and the monitoring of weather conditions and hardware health. We also discuss modeling techniques used to improve observing efficiency, including ensemble level focus modeling, which allows the array to conduct observations without requiring time-consuming focus runs. Finally, we describe the interconnected set of servers that enable realtime monitoring of observational performance.

Items.Authors: George G. Williams, William Goble, John DiMiceli, Ricardo Ortiz, Timothy Pickering, Benjamin J. Weiner
Items.Title: The 6.5-m MMT Telescope: current status and plans for the future
Items.Abstract: The 6.5-m MMT telescope has been in operation for more than 25 years and, as such, is a very reliable and productive general-purpose astronomical instrument. The telescope can be configured with one of three secondary mirrors that feed more than ten instruments at the Cassegrain focus. The MMT operates almost entirely in queue mode, and that has enabled a rapid response follow-up capability for observations of transient and multi-messenger sources. In this paper, we provide an overview of the telescope and the current suite of instruments, along with their capabilities and performance. Using various metrics, we summarize the productivity and impact of the observatory over the past 25 years. We also highlight recent efforts that have focused on maximizing the efficiency of observing and improving the delivered image quality. Finally, we will discuss plans for the future, including technical upgrades, instrument decommissioning, and new instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Diego Götz, Stefano Covino, Frédéric Pinsard, Aline Meuris, Eric Doumayrou, Thierry Tourette, Dehbia Lattab, Henri E. Triou, Samuel Ronayette, Luca Oggioni, Fabrizio Fornasiero, Stéphane Basa, Ludovic Genolet, Enrico Bozzo, Luca Terenzi, Karine Mercier, Lander Ruiz de Ocenda, Florent Robinet, Bortolino Saggin, Marco G. Corti, Christoph Tenzer, Paul Hedderman, Shaymaa Hussein, Lauro Conti, Mariachiara Celato, Viktor Toth, Andras P. Joo, Rebeka Kiss, Bendeguz Koncz, Adrien Fort, Jean-Michel Le Duigou
Items.Title: The IRT Telescope on board Theseus
Items.Abstract: We will present the Infra-Red Telescope (IRT), which is part of the payload of the THESEUS mission, currently undergoing a competitive phase A for the M7 mission slot of ESA (launch date 2037). The IRT is a 0.7m class telescope with an off-axis Korsch optical design, with imaging capabilities in the 0.7 to 1.8 microns range over a 15 x 15 arc min field of view. The IRT will provide also slitless low resolution spectoscopy (R~400) over a limited field of view of 2 x 2 arc min, in the 0.8-1.6 microns range. The goal of the IRT is to identify the NIR counterparts to the Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) detected by the two other telescopes on board THESEUS (the XGIS and the SXI), and tho mueasure on board its photmetric redshift in near real-time. The position and the redshift will be transmitted immediately to ground to allow for deeper follow-up by the large telescopes (ELT, VLT, ...). If the source is bright enough spectrocopy will be performed to charaterize the GRB environment.

Items.Authors: Andrea Bianco, Letizia Caito, Sofia Randich, Emma Fernandez Alvar, Oscar Gonzalez, Sergio Sousa, Thomas Bensby, Enrico Giro, Laura Magrini, Marco Riva
Items.Title: HRMOS: a very high-resolution, multi-object spectrograph for the ESO VLT
Items.Abstract: HRMOS (https://www.hrmos.eu/) is a new instrument we plan to propose for the European Southern Observatory Very Large Telescope. The original concept has matured into a solid design that combines very high spectral resolution (R = 80,000), multiplex capability (> 50 fibers), blue wavelength coverage down to 385 nm, and excellent radial velocity precision (requirement 10 m/s). With this unique combination, HRMOS will crucially fill the gap in the landscape of current and planned instrumentation, offering capabilities that are essential to address transformative science questions across a broad range of areas. The current concepts includes a number of innovative aspects. Also, the spectrograph design is devised to allow flexibility and possible future upgrades.     The talk will provide an overview of the instrument top level requirements, design and innovative technological solutions, feasibility and challenges.

Items.Authors: Haoran Li, Yao Hu, Qun Hao
Items.Title: Surface figure error and parameter testing of aspheric segments in segmented telescope primary mirrors
Items.Abstract: Segmented Telescope Primary Mirrors (STPMs) are a pivotal breakthrough in large-aperture optical engineering, addressing long-standing bottlenecks in manufacturing, transporting, and deploying monolithic large-diameter mirrors. For testing aspheric STPM segments during manufacturing and alignment, computer-generated hologram (CGH)-based interferometry is widely adopted for its high accuracy. However, centered and off-axis segments need different CGHs, often leading to overlooked aspheric parameter inconsistency (e.g., curvature radius), degrading STPMs’ overall performance. We propose a non-null interferometer for surface figure error and parameter testing, enabling shared measurement of all segments to ensure parameter consistency and better post-alignment performance. Experiments on a 400 mm aspheric mirror and simulations for meter-scale STPMs are presented.

Items.Authors: Ahmed Sanny, Lucas Labadie, Simon Gross, Kevin Barjot, Denis Defrère, Romain Laugier, Marc-Antoine Martinod, Germain Garreau, Thomas Mattheussen, Peter Marley Chingaipe, Michael Withford
Items.Title: Asgard/NOTT: the performance of the integrated optics 4-telescope beam combiner for double-Bracewell nulling interferometry
Items.Abstract: The core of the Asgard/NOTT visitor instrument for mid-infrared L′-band nulling interferometry is an integrated optics beam combiner called the 4T-nuller. It is manufactured using ultrafast laser inscription and has been tested for on-sky performance with an interferometric test bench that generates four coherent beams simultaneously, simulating VLTI operations. The 4T-nuller features three cascaded achromatic directional couplers in its interferometric section, along with Y-junctions for routing signals to the photometry section. Its total throughput is 37%, accounting for Fresnel losses, and it shows low differential birefringence. Under ambient conditions without polarization control, we measured an average broadband raw null of 8.13±0.03×10⁻³ and a self-calibrated null of 1.14±0.01×10⁻³ over 20 seconds. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a deep null in the L′-band using an integrated-optics beam combiner that also meets the requirements of the NOTT.

Items.Authors: Takafumi Tsukui
Items.Title: From visibilities to functions: rethinking data management for giant arrays
Items.Abstract: Next-generation interferometers will produce massive data, making it impractical to store the original visibility measurements and later combine the observations in uv spatial frequency space. Such datasets would incur high storage costs and environmental impact. We propose modelling the highly redundant visibility measurements using a sparse Gaussian process (GP) model and storing the compact model rather than raw visibilities. We found that the approximate GP is flexible enough to represent the visibilities and recover images with high fidelity. The optimisation exploits correlations in uv space, potentially boosting the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) compared with grid averaging. Once trained, the mean visibility and its uncertainty can be computed at any desired (u, v) coordinates. The model may be incrementally updated with new observations, while filtering out outliers based on the prediction. We discuss the resulting data-volume reduction, image fidelity, and future directions.

Items.Authors: Aleksej Kiselev, Martin Timpe, Matthias Reichert, Tony Mroczkowski, Claudia Cicone
Items.Title: Simulation-based dynamic pointing analysis of AtLAST under wind loading and fast-scan conditions
Items.Abstract: The Atacama Large Aperture Submillimeter Telescope (AtLAST) is designed for high-speed, wide-field submillimeter mapping, which requires excellent dynamic pointing performance under wind loading and fast-scan operation. We present a simulation framework that couples a detailed structural model with a realistic multi-loop telescope drive control system. Wind excitation is derived from high-resolution site measurements, while self-induced effects are studied using realistic fast-scan patterns such as Lissajous-daisy trajectories at the mount’s kinematic limits. The simulations show that, for all tested wind conditions, total dynamic pointing remains within the allocated budgets and is dominated by a residual term driven by structural flexibility. During fast scans, however, the error is mainly set by finite control bandwidth. This decomposition guides structural and control design choices and informs future active compensation strategies.

Items.Authors: Paul Szypryt, Douglas A. Bennett, Ian Fogarty Florang, Joseph W. Fowler, Andrea Giachero, Adriana E. Lita, John A. B. Mates, Galen C. O'Neil, Daniel S. Swetz, Leaf A. Swordy, Joel N. Ullom, Michael R. Vissers, Jordan Wheeler
Items.Title: Toward high spectral resolution transition-edge sensor arrays with highly scalable readouts for visible to near-infrared astronomy
Items.Abstract: Superconducting detectors operating in the visible to near-infrared regime have great potential for future space missions such as the Habitable Words Observatory (HWO). In particular, transition-edge sensor (TES) based microcalorimeters can be advantageous due to their high quantum efficiency across a broad range, moderate energy resolution, high maximum count rate, and low dark count rate. Unfortunately, the realized spectral resolution of these devices has been far below fundamental limits. Furthermore, developing highly multiplexed readouts for TES calorimeters at these wavelengths has been challenging. Here, we present on our progress on addressing these challenges. In particular, we introduce TES calorimeters with ultrathin membranes for increased phonon trapping. We also present progress on the highly scalable kinetic inductance current sensor (KICS), which replaces the superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) in the TES readout circuit.

Items.Authors: Jonas B. Ohland, Leon Dauerer, Nathalie Lebas, Vincent Deo, Olivier Guyon, Dimitris Papadopoulos, Vincent Bagnoud
Items.Title: AO for laser fusion: the challenges of controlling hundreds of high-power laser beams
Items.Abstract: Laser-driven inertial fusion is progressing quickly, but scaling from landmark ignition shots to an energy-relevant driver is an interdisciplinary problem, where one important part is linked to laser beam-control. This talk connects fusion-driver requirements to adaptive optics: how thermal load, air turbulence, alignment sensitivity and practical operation considerations translate into engineering challenges when many hundreds of high-energy beamlines must run reliably and repeatably. Using the Apollon Real-Time Adaptive Optics (ARTAO) experience, I outline what it takes to run AO loops robustly in a multi-petawatt laser hall, and introduce the ALADIN project, which is developing scalable control architectures that integrate sensing, correction, and automation for future fusion-laser systems.

Items.Authors: Tobias M. Schmidt, Gaspare Lo Curto, François Bouchy, Sebastian Schäfer, Michael Debus, Ansgar Reiners
Items.Title: Impact of fiber illumination geometry on wavelength calibration for high-resolution spectrographs
Items.Abstract: When pushing for the highest wavelength calibration accuracy (<1m/s) and radial-velocity stability (<10cm/s), subtle effects of the line-spread function (LSF) become increasingly important. We recently discovered adverse effects related to the fiber illumination geometry, at the front-end but also in the calibration unit.  To shed light on this, experiments with ESPRESSO were conducted, feeding light from the same laser frequency comb via different input ports of the calibration unit. We present observed differences in the near- and far-fields, as well as the impact on spectrum and wavelength calibration. This is complemented by dedicated laboratory measurements. Although many aspects of fiber-illumination and its impact on wavelength calibration and radial-velocity measurements remain puzzling, it is obvious that improvements to the light-guiding and scrambling are necessary to ensure a homogeneous and stable illumination of the spectrograph, for which we will give recommendations.

Items.Authors: Christian Veillet, Elena Masciadri, Camilo Weinberger, Sam Ragland, Juan Carlos Guerra
Items.Title: Implementation of an ensemble of atmospheric monitoring equipment at the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory site for agile AO-based observing, improved atmospheric turbulence forecasting, and local turbulence exploration
Items.Abstract: With two 8.4m main mirrors, a baseline of 24m in interferometric mode, two adaptive secondaries, and a growing suite of AO-fed instruments, LBT is truly the first of the ELTs. Relying heavily on AO, LBT’s observing strategy, as agile as possible, requires both forecasting and real-time monitoring of the atmospheric turbulence. So far, LBT has relied on a DIMM riding with the telescope inside the LBT enclosure, and ALTA has provided a daily forecast adjusted in real time to the DIMM data. In order to disentangle the atmospheric turbulence from local effects and to better monitor seeing in real time, thus improving the prediction model, a Polaris seeing monitor is now providing seeing data and a RINGSS turbulence profiler (providing tau0 and theta0) is being deployed. The first months of data will be presented, potentially hinting at local effects such as enclosure temperature and wind-induced turbulence around the building, and providing data as a real-life test bed of an ELT modeling.

Items.Authors: Stefan Kraus, Daniel Lancaster, Sorabh Chhabra, Jyotirmay Paul, Owain Snaith, Narsireddy Anugu, John Monnier, Michael Ireland, Adam Taras, Andrea Bianco, Michele Frangiamore
Items.Title: Opening short wavelengths for VLTI: Asgard/BIFROST project status and results from AIV and commissioning
Items.Abstract: BIFROST, part of the Asgard Suite of VLTI visitor instruments, is a short-wavelength, high-spectral resolution instrument optimized for spectral line studies in the Y, J, and H bands (1.05–1.75 μm). It will open the short-wavelength window for VLTI and cover unique atomic and molecular spectral lines. This presentation reviews BIFROST’s science drivers and how they shaped its operational modes. AIV and on-sky commissioning of the on-axis arm and low-resolution spectrograph are planned for March–April 2026, enabling first commissioning results at SPIE to assess performance and highlight remaining challenges. We outline milestones toward the off-axis module and high-resolution spectrograph commissioning in early 2027, and discuss ongoing BIFROST-related activities aimed at future upgrades.

Items.Authors: Schuyler G. Wolff, Vanessa Bailey, Justin Hom, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Susan F. Redmond, Julien H. Girard, Oscar Carrión-González, Dmitry Savransky, Johan Mazoyer, Macarena Vega-Pallauta, Gael Chauvin, Matthieu Ravet, Alexandra Greenbaum, Eric Cady, Ramya M. Anche, James G. Ingalls
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: trials and triumphs of designing an observing program for a technology demonstration instrument
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraph Instrument onboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope serves as a crucial technology pathfinder for the Habitable Worlds Observatory, with on-sky verification of high-contrast imaging techniques and the potential to image a Jupiter analog for the first time. Together with the Roman Project Team, the Community Participation Program (CPP) is responsible for target selection, preparatory observations, developing an exposure time calculator, target database, data reduction pipeline, simulation tools, and engagement with the broader community. Here we present an overview of the CPP activities over the past two years with an emphasis on observation planning activities for the initial in-orbit checkout and the first six months of the observation phase. Finally, we present future opportunities for the astronomical community to interact with the data as it becomes public early in the mission.

Items.Authors: Lydia Stofanova, Norbert Werner, Filip Munz, Jakub Rípa, Vladimír Dániel, Zsolt Varhegyi, Giancarlo Ghirlanda, Giovanni Pareschi, Jan Vaclavik, Ehud Behar, Suresh Sivanandam, Aaron Tohuvavohu, Mark Barnet
Items.Title: Mission overview of QUVIK: the first Czech-led space telescope and its science case
Items.Abstract: QUVIK - Quick Ultra-Violet Kilonova surveyor - is a Czech-led science and technology mission being developed under the auspices of the European Space Agency. The mission will provide key follow-up capabilities to increase the discovery potential of gravitational wave observatories and future wide-field multi-wavelength surveys. The primary objective of the mission is the measurement of the ultraviolet (UV) brightness evolution of kilonovae, resulting from mergers of neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole. To understand their nature and explosion scenarios, information about their UV brightness shortly after the explosion is needed. This missing link will be provided by QUVIK. The mission also provides follow-up capabilities for other transients. Its wide range of scientific goals (kilonovae, supernovae, GRB afterglows, exoplanets, stars, active galactic nuclei etc.) will be reinforced by the unique capability to perform simultaneous observation in the near- and far-UV bands.

Items.Authors: Michiel van der Hoeven, Arturo Nunez, Felipe Daruich, Patrick Dunlop, Elka Koehler
Items.Title: NOIRLab five Years into integrated operations in engineering
Items.Abstract: NOIRLab 5 Years into Integrated Operations in Engineering    This paper describes how the engineering division has evolved during its initial 5 years of operation under NOIRLab to optimally serve both operational and developmental requirements across its observatories.     NSF NOIRLab (formally named the National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory) is the US national center for ground-based, nighttime optical astronomy. It operates five Programs — NSF Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), the Community Science and Data Center (CSDC), the International Gemini Observatory, NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO) and NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory.     The engineering division operates in a matrixed organizational structure to serve its five programs. This paper details the journey, presenting key lessons learned, successful strategies, and areas targeted for improvement.

Items.Authors: Lorenzo Pettazzi, Martin Dimmler, Mauro Tuti, Omar Sqalli, Andreas Foerster, Marc Cayrel
Items.Title: Serial production in the context of ground-based astronomy projects: the ELT M1 case
Items.Abstract: The M1 is, without a doubt, one of the most impressive subsystems within the ELT telescope. The endeavor of building such a masterpiece of technology is tightly linked to the challenges of designing, developing and producing in series the hundreds or thousands of components that constitute the gigantic active mirror. This manuscript focuses on the description of the multiple challenges that ESO and its industrial partners have faced to ensure that the design of the M1 components was properly engineered for serial production, to set up the production facilities and to maintain the specified production quality and yield over the years. Finally the paper will describe the multiple solutions adopted in the different projects to overcome the challenges and reflects on the lessons learned during the process.

Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: pre-launch reference star list and impact of reference star properties on post-processing performance
Items.Abstract: The upcoming Roman Coronagraph aims to directly image and characterize exoplanetary systems at contrasts higher than 10^-7, a key technological milestone for Habitable Worlds Observatory coronagraph development. Doing so requires alternating observations of science targets and bright reference stars. These reference stars must satisfy strict criteria, including being single star systems. Other reference star attributes may have other impacts on post-processing performance on a case-by-case basis. Only a small number of the brightest stars in the sky are potentially suitable, necessitating precursor observations and simulations to validate their use. We will present the pre-launch list of Roman Coronagraph reference stars informed from an extensive observing campaign. We will also present the results of simulations investigating the impact of reference star properties on post-processing performance. We discuss the importance of reference star selection for scheduling and performance.

Items.Authors: Sven Herrmann, Peter Orel, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Haley R. Stueber, Abigail Y. Pan, Kevan A. Donlon, Declan O'Neill, Jill Juneau, Eric D. Miller, R. Glenn Morris, Artem Poliszczuk, Beverly J. LaMarr, Catherine E. Grant, Christopher W. Leitz, Steven W. Allen, Sebastian Albrecht, Marshall W. Bautz, Michael J. Cooper, Ajay K. Dakshinamurthy, Matthew Heine, Gregory Y. Prigozhin, Anna Schweingruber, Keith Warner, Daniel R. Wilkins
Items.Title: Fast low-noise megapixel detector and readout systems for future x-ray astronomy missions
Items.Abstract: State-of-the-art X-ray CCDs are close to delivering the key performance metrics for the next generation of X-ray telescope except the required frame rates. Our group at Stanford is addressing these technology gaps, in collaboration with colleagues at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and MIT Lincoln Laboratory (MIT-LL). To meet this need, we are developing advanced multichannel readout electronics that utilize microelectronics, waveform sampling, and digital signal processing in an FPGA. First operation with a large 2 Mpixel MIT-LL CCD was achieved and demonstrates the performance of this architecture. We also report progress on our continued development of the novel SiSeRO (Single electron Sensitive Read Out) technology, which can deliver substantially sub-electron noise at competitive readout speeds. Finally, we discuss the development of AI methods to enhance our detector performance, including enhanced particle background screening and improved event characterization.

Items.Authors: Vladimír Dániel, Norbert Werner, Lydia Štofanová, Jakub Řípa, Filip Munz, Zsolt Varhegyi
Items.Title: Quick Ultra-VIolet Kilonova surveyor (QUVIK) spacecraft and payloads design update
Items.Abstract: The QUVIK mission, designed for rapid ultraviolet (UV) observations of kilonovae and gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) afterglows, has advanced significantly since its initial design review. Updates include an orbit and operations concept with common 10:30 LTDN, enabling observations during orbital eclipse phases while daylight is reserved for charging and data downlink. The pointing budget and point spread function (PSF) are now integrated into a refined performance model with multiple utilisation scenarios. Instrument baselines for near-UV (NUV) and far-UV (FUV) bands have been optimised for better sensitivity and throughput. Rapid gamma-ray localisation follow-up is supported by the presence of a GRB detector with localisation capabilities. This paper summarises the current spacecraft and payload accommodation and highlights how these updates enhance QUVIK’s capability for rapid UV transient detection.

Items.Authors: John Romein, Ewan Barr, Ilse van Bemmel, Wiebe van Breukelen, Théo Chicard, Willem-Jan Dirks, Niclas Esser, Hugh Garsden, André Gunst, Valentin Hazard, Aard Keimpema, Mark Kettenis, Corné Lukken, Jan David Mol, Leon Oostrum, Vishambhar Nath Pandey, Matīss Purviņš, Benjamin Quertier, Ronald Rook, Theotime Sergeant, Karina Šķirmante, Jānis Šteinbergs, Gie Han Tan, Bram Veenboer, Marjolein Verkouter, Eric Villard, Steven van der Vlugt
Items.Title: RADIOBLOCKS: High-performance building blocks for GPU correlators
Items.Abstract: In this session, we present RADIOBLOCKS: a collection of highly optimized GPU signal-processing libraries, that form the building blocks for a new generation of radio-astronomical correlator and beam-former applications. We also describe new methods to efficiently transfer data from FPGA digitizers near the antennas into GPU correlator systems, at high data rates. Then, we show how these "radio blocks" and I/O methods are deployed in (upgrades of) correlator/beam-former applications for a variety of radio telescopes. Finally, we present the new ALMA WSU digitizer.

Items.Authors: Nicholas E. White, Massimiliano Galeazzi, Daniel Kocevski, J. Eric Grove, Sylvain Guiriec, Alexander J. van der Horst, Russell Roberts, Brendan O'Connor, Paul S. Ray, Dheeraj Pasham, Peter Roming
Items.Title: XTRA: the x-ray transient array
Items.Abstract: XTRA (X-ray TRansient Array) is a NASA Small Explorer concept designed for 2030s time-domain and multi-messenger astrophysics. Operating in a Sun-Earth L2 orbit, XTRA makes time-domain surveys and provides rapid autonomous response to high-energy transients. The payload combines the Burst Alert Monitor (BAM)—a broadband (50 keV–2 MeV) gamma-ray monitor for continuous triggering—with the Micropore Optics X-ray Instrument (MOXI)—a wide-field (240 sq deg) soft X-ray (0.2–5 keV) imager for rapid arcminute localization. Surveying the anti-Sun nighttime hemisphere on a variety of cadences, XTRA acts as the high-energy anchor for the 2030s ecosystem, feeding triggers to robotic telescopes for immediate counterpart identification. XTRA will decode cosmic explosions (GRBs, shock breakouts), trace black hole feeding via tidal disruption events (TDEs), and uncover electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational wave and high-energy neutrino sources.

Items.Authors: Arjo Bos, Pim van Wershoven, Bart Speet, Fred Kamphues, Wouter Jonker
Items.Title: Sensitivity analysis and design of a segmented active M1 for the next-generation telescopes
Items.Abstract: In the current generation of Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs), relatively thick segmented M1 mirror segments are applied. These mirror segments of significant mass have complex mechanical support structures that warp and co-phase each element such that a single mirror surface is achieved. TNO believes that with recent developments, the next-generation telescopes can be made possible by decreasing mass, making the M1 segments active (or even adaptive), and significantly decreasing the cost of the glass mirror segments.   In this paper we present a sensitivity analysis and concept design of a segmented active thin-shell M1 segment for the next-generation telescopes. Multiple applications are foreseen, from retrofitting existing telescopes such as a 15m 'Keck 2.0', application in the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), or even a 60+ meter ELT.

Items.Authors: Marianne Cox, Jose M. Filgueira, Chien Peng, Jordi Molgó, Hector Swett, Jorge Barrios, Paulo H. Silva, William Baumgartner, Jenna Snead, Brian Hicks
Items.Title: Observatory software management in the era of AI-assisted software engineering
Items.Abstract: Thanks to advancements in generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), the last 5 years has seen exponential growth in the adoption of AI-Assisted software engineering across many industries. Simple developer tools used for code completion, static analysis and syntax linting have been augmented by agent-assisted development and autonomous coding. The way we develop, analyze and test software is rapidly changing.   At GMTO, we stand to benefit from these technologies and adopting industry best practices. However, it needs to be  done in a way that carefully considers our unique concerns and risks. In this paper we describe how we are starting to utilize AI-assisted software engineering at GMTO, why these common industry concerns matter for Observatory software teams, and future plans.

Items.Authors: Julien H. Girard, Eric Cady, Neil T. Zimmerman, Gael Chauvin, Vanessa Bailey, Ruslan Belikov, Beth Biller, Sarah Blunt, Jessica Gersh-Range, Justin Hom, Masayuki Kuzuhara, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Matthias Samland, Dan Sirbu, Macarena Vega-Pallauta, Schuyler G. Wolff, Jason Wang, Jingwen Zhang
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: end to end preparation of a pilot observation of a moderate contrast companion
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraph Instrument, technology pathfinder, is ready to fly onboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a NASA flagship mission scheduled to launch before the Spring 2027. The Community Participation Program (CPP) is building a comprehensive observing program for the “Coronagraph” with preparation, calibration and data processing software. Here we describe a sub-program that could be carried out as soon as the instrument is operational and high-order wavefront sensing and control has been exercised successfully. This program would generate the first canonical on-sky dataset of a bright star with an easily recoverable self luminous companion. We show all preparation steps using the whole suite of tools developed by the CPP. This “training” dataset will be precious for the readiness of the technology demonstration at higher contrasts and for our community to subsequently tackle more difficult targets, including giant exoplanets in reflected light.

Items.Authors: Heidi Schweiker, William McBride, Pipa Fernandez
Items.Title: Using field mills to monitor atmospheric electric fields for lightning safety at observatories
Items.Abstract: For remote mountain-top observatories, lightning is a considerable risk to personnel and hardware. Conventional lightning warnings are often inaccurate or too late for a timely response. In order to get a more precise indication of the potential for a lightning strike, we have installed field mills to monitor the electric fields in the atmosphere above Kitt Peak National Observatory. Regularly in use for rocket launches and (previously) the Space Shuttle, field mills can indicate a buildup of electrical charge, which is a known precursor to a lightning strike. We will discuss the deployment and integration of our field mills with our mountain operations, the development of thresholds for automatic broadcast alerts and safety precautions we have incorporated in response to these alerts. Based on our experience we will present how other observatories can benefit from incorporating similar electric field monitoring systems into their operations and safety programs.

Items.Authors: Bernadett Stadler, Guido Agapito, Ollie Farley, Noelia Martinez Rey, Alfio Puglisi, Fabio Rossi, Roberto Biasi, Domenico Bonaccini Calia, David Jenkins, Daniel Jodlbauer, Ramon Mata Calvo, James Osborn, Felipe Pedreros Bustos
Items.Title: End-to-end adaptive optics simulations for predicting the performance of bidirectional optical feeder links
Items.Abstract: Space optical laser communication represents a technological challenge. Atmospheric turbulence disturbs the uplink and downlink laser beams, thus, strongly limiting the achievable data throughput. In this talk we focus on the prediction of the performance improvement when employing Adaptive Optics (AO) systems for the optical communication with GEO and LEO satellites using numerical end-to-end simulations. In particular, we show results for the ALASCA project, which develops an optical communication channel from the ESA optical ground station in Tenerife to communication satellites using the Laser Guide Star AO (LGS-AO) concept. The simulations are carried out using SPECULA, which is a Python-based end-to-end AO software tool developed at INAF Arcetri for astronomical applications that has been adapted for the use in optical communication. The reliability of the simulations is guaranteed through cross-validation with other numerical and analytical simulators as well as on-sky results.

Items.Authors: Patrick Côté, Tyrone E. Woods, Matthew A. Taylor, John S. Pazder
Items.Title: Progress report on the CASTOR mission
Items.Abstract: We present a progress report on the CASTOR mission. CASTOR is a proposed 1m-diameter, wide-field space telescope that is under development by the National Research Council of Canada and the Canadian Space Agency. The mission utilizes a three-mirror anastigmat design to deliver high-resolution imaging (FWHM ~0.15”) over a ~0.25 square degree field simultaneously in three channels: UV (150-300nm), u (300-400nm) and g (400-550nm). The telescope will be mounted on the Magellan MAC-200 small-SAT bus, and placed into a sun-synchronous dawn-dusk orbit at an altitude of roughly 800 km. According to the current development schedule, launch would occur in the early 2030s.    The mission design is optimized for panoramic imaging in three simultaneous channels covering the UV/blue-optical wavelength range. Additional observing modes include: (1) wide-field, slit-less (grism) spectroscopy between 150 and 400 nm; (2) precision photometry for exoplanet transit measurements; and (3) DMD-based UV multi-

Items.Authors: Sebastian Schäfer, Michael Debus, Tobias Schmidt, Vitalii Kostogryz, Ansgar Reiners
Items.Title: Toward a community framework for illumination stability in EPRV spectrographs
Items.Abstract: As extreme-precision RV spectrographs push toward the 10 cm/s regime, illumination stability has become a dominant but poorly quantified limitation. At present, every major EPRV instrument team develops its own set of scrambling metrics, fiber tests, and modal-noise mitigation strategies. These efforts have led to impressive individual results, but they are not directly comparable, and they do not yet form a transferable framework that new instruments can adopt without repeating large parts of the experimental work.  We introduce an effort to establish reproducible illumination metrics. Rather than instrument-specific tests, we will map illumination behaviour across a broad range of wavelengths, source types, fibers, and launch conditions to capture the diversity of real systems. Our goal is to provide illumination metrics and guidelines that can be shared, compared, and reused, reducing duplicated effort and supporting the design of future high-precision radial-velocity instruments.

Items.Authors: Michael Pleasance
Items.Title: Correlator/beamformer for the Square Kilometre Array Mid Frequency Telescope: design and status update
Items.Abstract: The National Research Council of Canada (NRC) is leading the development and delivery of the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) Mid Frequency Correlator/Beamformer (Mid.CBF) signal processing system. This talk provides an overview of the system design for both the early prototype systems (TALON Demonstration Correlator) and production systems for the larger array assemblies. The talk also provides a status update, highlighting completed and upcoming milestones.
